newsitem.title: EAST TIMOR: FEATURE - East Timor brews up organic coffee industry.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - East Timor brews up organic coffee industry.

text.p: In the hip cafes of America's West Coast, Europe and Australia, troubled East Timor is more likely to be the topic of discussion than home to the brew beneath the fluff of the cappuccino.
But from the hills of this remote and rugged former Portuguese colony, birthplace of last year's Noble peace prize winners, there is talk of a new taste -- naturally grown and worth savouring.
"The cachet is certainly there, but you can't last long in the market without providing a good cup of coffee," Sam Filiaci, one of the main movers behind the Timor coffee project, said.

While small bands of guerrillas still fight in the hills for independence more than 21 years after Indonesia absorbed East Timor, thousands of small farmers are eagerly signing up to join the new movement of organic farming.
Certification as organic farmers allows them to tap into a lucrative market for a clean produce in places far removed from the sleepy enclave in the tropics just north of Australia.
COFFEE FARMERS GIVE EXCEPTIONAL RESPONSE

"The response has been exceptional. In our first year, in a trial programme, we started with just 700 farmers," Filiaci, country director of the U.S.-based National Cooperative Business Association (NCBA), said.
It is the NCBA, together with local cooperatives, which run what is known as the Timor Coffee Project, a programme funded by the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID).
"In the second year, we targeted about 2,500 farmers and we had to cut off at 6,700. This year we plan to get between 9,000 - 10,000," Filiaci told Reuters recently.
The enthusiasm is easily accounted for in one of the poorest regions in the Indonesian archipelago.
"It comes down to money. Organic coffee in a strong market will pay between 15-20 percent, and in a weak market 10-15 percent more than similar coffee," Filiaci said.
TIMOR'S TROUBLES CREATE HISTORICAL ACCIDENT

Ironically, the territory's troubles have played a part in keeping the Arabica coffee trees of thousands of small farmers free from pesticide and fertilizer use, making it ideal as a source of organically-grown Arabica coffee.

Like Nicaragua and El Salvador, where the NCBA has also worked, guerrilla activity in the mountains kept government extension officers, who would have promoted pesticide and fertilizer use, far from the coffee growing districts.
"The farmer's did not use any pesticides or fertilizers. This meant we were able to get certification without a mandatory three-year probation period," Filiaci said.
"We were fortunate in Central America as, because of warfare, for several years the farmers there did not use pesticides and fertilizers," he said.
The same applied to East Timor, he added.
VYING WITH INDONESIAN COMPETITORS

Timor's Arabica bean, known as Hibrido de Timor, grown on fertile volcanic soils and in high humidity, is vying with the already popular boutique Arabicas from Indonesia's main islands of Java and Sumatra, as well as the mountain enclave of Toraja on Sulawesi island.

It is likely new names could soon enter the coffee drinkers' lexicon. East Timor's premium crop comes from the hills around Maubessi, where trees grow at elevations between of 1,300 and 1,800 metres (4,300 and 5,900 feet). Other key centres are around Ermera and Liquica.
Certification by the Ohio-based Organic Crop Improvement Association (OCIA) that gives the product an edge, also brings higher returns to East Timor's farmers who are among the poorest in the region.
But the Timor coffee project, given five years of start-up funding by the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), has wrought more change than just filling the farmers' pockets.
The project broke the coffee monopoly run by people associated with the powerful Indonesian military, which has largely run East Timor since 1976.
EXPORT SUCCESS MEANS JOBS
In a nondescript but aromatic wharehouse in downtown Dili, the immediate benefits of the project in a place known for its troubling unemployment are clear.

More than 100 workers bustle among the sacks of coffee stacked to the ceiling as men lug the freshly harvested crop in and out of grading machines before women and girls sort the best of the green beans for export.
In the hills, another 500 people are employed for five months a year in the weighing stations and wet processing facilities.
The project, still in an experiental stage, produced only 50 tonnes of premium coffeee from the 1995 season. Filiaci said the 1996 season will yield 600 tonnes of high-grade export product.

The most recent government statistics show the 25,177 coffee farming families of East Timor's 13 regencies produced 8,450 tonnes of mostly Arabica coffee in 1995, a slight fall from the 8,799 tonnes produced the previous year.
"We're playing it by ear, but we think that a good long-term goal for us is about 3,000 tonnes considering factors in East Timor. We're shooting for this at the end of five years," Filiaci said.
